title: Networking Domain 2: Routing, Switching, VLANs & Wireless (20%)
overview: Covers VLAN tagging/trunking, Spanning Tree (STP), link aggregation (LACP), routing protocols, and Wi-Fi standards.
art: WI-FI NON-OVERLAPPING CHANNELS (2.4 GHz)      WIFI STANDARDS

1.label: VLANs, Access Ports vs. 802.1Q Trunk Ports
1.what: VLANs (Virtual LANs) logically split one physical switch into multiple isolated broadcast domains for security and performance.
1.exam_facts: Access Port: Carries traffic for ONE single VLAN (connects to PCs/printers). Trunk Port (IEEE 802.1Q): Carries multiple VLANs simultaneously between switches/routers by inserting a 4-byte VLAN tag. Native VLAN carries untagged traffic (default VLAN 1—change it for security!).
1.troubleshoot: Inter-VLAN Routing: Devices in VLAN 10 cannot talk to VLAN 20 without a Layer 3 Switch (SVI) or a Router ('Router-on-a-Stick' using sub-interfaces). Always check for Native VLAN mismatches on trunk ports!

2.label: Switch Redundancy: STP (802.1D/w) & LACP (802.3ad)
2.what: Redundant cables between switches prevent single points of failure, but require protocols to prevent broadcast storms or bundle bandwidth.
2.exam_facts: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP / RSTP 802.1w): Elects a Root Bridge (lowest Bridge ID = Priority + MAC) and puts redundant ports into a Blocking/Discarding state to prevent Layer 2 loops. LACP (802.3ad / EtherChannel): Bonds multiple physical cables into one high-speed logical link.
2.troubleshoot: If a switch CPU spikes to 100% and all port LEDs blink rapidly in unison, you likely have a Layer 2 switching loop because STP was disabled or misconfigured.

3.label: Routing Protocols, Administrative Distance & NAT/PAT
3.what: Routers forward packets between different IP networks using static routes or dynamic routing protocols.
3.exam_facts: IGP (Interior): OSPF (Link-State, uses Dijkstra's algorithm, fast convergence, metric = Cost/bandwidth) vs RIP (Distance-Vector, metric = Hop count, max 15 hops). EGP (Exterior): BGP (Path-Vector, runs the global Internet, uses ASNs). FHRP: VRRP/HSRP provide a Virtual IP for default-gateway redundancy.
3.troubleshoot: NAT vs PAT: Static NAT maps 1 private IP to 1 public IP. PAT (NAT Overload) maps thousands of private IPs to ONE public IP by tracking unique source port numbers.

4.label: Wireless Standards (802.11), Frequencies & Security
4.what: Connects wireless clients via Access Points (WAPs) across 2.4 GHz (longer range, penetrates walls, slower, crowded) and 5 GHz / 6 GHz (faster, shorter range, more channels).
4.exam_facts: 2.4 GHz has ONLY 3 non-overlapping 20MHz channels: 1, 6, and 11. Standards: 802.11n (Wi-Fi 4 - 2.4/5GHz), 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5 - 5GHz only, MU-MIMO), 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6/6E - OFDMA, 2.4/5/6GHz). Security: WPA2-Enterprise (802.1X/RADIUS + AES-CCMP) or WPA3 (SAE - prevents offline dictionary attacks).
4.troubleshoot: Co-channel interference happens when nearby APs use the same channel; Adjacent-channel interference happens when APs use overlapping channels like 2, 3, or 4—stick strictly to 1, 6, and 11 on 2.4 GHz!
